title: Bronchiectasis: Chronic Suppurative Airway Disease Needs a Cause and a Culture Strategy
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is more than recurrent cough. Confirm structural airway dilation, identify treatable causes and microbiology, support airway clearance, and recognize exacerbation or hemoptysis that requires urgent escalation rather than repeatedly prescribing empiric antibiotics without a longitudinal plan.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, daily sputum and intermittent hemoptysis should raise suspicion, especially when symptoms persist between infections.
Frequent exacerbations, weight loss, clubbing, crackles or prior severe/recurrent infections increase concern for established structural disease.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist, but bronchiectasis requires structural airway abnormality rather than airflow symptoms alone.
Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiency, aspiration, inflammatory disease, prior infection and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease are important etiologic considerations.
assessment: Characterize sputum quantity/colour, exacerbation frequency, prior organisms, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight/nutrition, reflux/aspiration clues, sinus disease, autoimmune symptoms and prior severe infections.
Review smoking/vaping exposure, vaccination, inhaled therapies, airway-clearance technique and previous microbiology including Pseudomonas when present.
workup: High-resolution chest CT is central to confirming bronchiectasis when clinically suspected.

Obtain sputum culture during meaningful exacerbations and when establishing microbiologic history; use targeted testing for immune deficiency, ABPA, CF/PCD or other causes when the presentation warrants it.
Pulmonary function testing helps characterize physiology and trend disease but does not replace structural confirmation.
management: Teach and reinforce an individualized airway-clearance regimen, ideally with respiratory physiotherapy expertise.
Treat exacerbations using prior/current microbiology, severity and local antimicrobial guidance rather than defaulting to the same empiric antibiotic each time.

Refer to respirology for recurrent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas, significant hemoptysis, progressive lung-function decline, uncertain etiology or consideration of long-term inhaled/macrolide/specialty therapy.
medicationSafety: Before long-term macrolide therapy, confirm specialist-guided indication and review QT, hearing, interactions and nontuberculous mycobacterial risk.
Inhaled corticosteroids are not routine bronchiectasis therapy unless another indication such as asthma/selected COPD features exists.
redFlags: Rapidly worsening symptoms despite appropriate therapy
New focal chest pain or concern for pulmonary embolism/pneumothorax
counselling: Explain that daily airway clearance and microbiology-guided care reduce the cycle of retained secretions and infection.
Provide an exacerbation action plan and smoking/vaping cessation support where relevant.
followUp: Track exacerbation frequency, sputum microbiology, lung function, hemoptysis and weight/nutrition.
Close the loop on etiologic testing because identifying immune, allergic, aspiration or genetic contributors can materially change treatment.
examTrap: Treating every productive-cough flare with the same antibiotic without confirming bronchiectasis, reviewing prior cultures or addressing airway clearance.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is airway clearance plus microbiology plus cause—not antibiotics alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Non-CF Bronchiectasis working-group/current respiratory guidance

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize the Syndrome, Find the Group, Refer Early
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes, not a single drug diagnosis. Suspect it in unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart findings, look for left-heart/lung/thromboembolic disease, obtain appropriate echocardiographic assessment, and refer suspected pulmonary arterial or chronic thromboembolic disease to an expert pathway before disease-specific therapy.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pressure, presyncope/syncope, edema and reduced exercise tolerance can be presenting features.
Elevated JVP, right-ventricular heave, loud P2, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly or hypoxemia suggest more advanced right-heart involvement.
differentiate: Common pulmonary-hypertension mechanisms include left-heart disease, chronic lung/hypoxic disease and chronic thromboembolic disease; pulmonary arterial hypertension is a more specialized subgroup.
A high estimated pulmonary pressure on echocardiography is not itself a definitive hemodynamic diagnosis and does not replace specialist interpretation/right-heart catheterization when indicated.
assessment: Assess functional limitation, syncope, edema, chest symptoms, VTE history, connective-tissue disease, portal disease, HIV/drug exposure, congenital heart disease, sleep-disordered breathing and chronic lung/left-heart disease.
Pregnancy or pregnancy planning is a high-risk context that requires early specialist coordination.
workup: Initial evaluation commonly includes ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography, oxygenation, pulmonary function and cause-directed laboratory testing.
When chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension is possible, use the appropriate pulmonary-vascular imaging pathway rather than assuming a normal routine chest CT excludes it.
Right-heart catheterization is the definitive hemodynamic test when specialist evaluation indicates it.
management: Treat hypoxemia and the underlying left-heart, lung, sleep or thromboembolic disease when identified.

Refer suspected pulmonary arterial hypertension or chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension to a pulmonary-vascular expert centre; disease-specific vasodilator therapy should not be started empirically for undifferentiated pulmonary hypertension.
Acute right-heart decompensation requires monitored hospital-level management and careful attention to preload, oxygenation and precipitating causes.
medicationSafety: Pulmonary vasodilators can worsen some patients with left-heart or lung disease and require specialist indication.
Anticoagulation decisions depend on the underlying pulmonary-hypertension group and thromboembolic context rather than the pressure estimate alone.
redFlags: Pregnancy with suspected significant pulmonary hypertension
Concern for acute or chronic thromboembolic disease
counselling: Explain that the next step is determining why pulmonary pressure is elevated, because treatment differs substantially by cause.
Give explicit urgent-care advice for syncope, rapidly worsening dyspnea, chest pain or edema.
followUp: Ensure specialist referral, pending imaging and etiologic testing are closed-loop.
Track functional class, oxygenation, edema and right-heart symptoms while definitive classification is underway.
examTrap: Starting pulmonary-arterial-hypertension medication because an echocardiogram reports elevated pulmonary pressure before establishing the cause and hemodynamics.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a classification problem before it is a prescribing problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Thoracic Society Position Statement on Pulmonary Hypertension
Canadian Thoracic Society Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension guidance

title: Sarcoidosis: Compatible Pattern, Exclusion of Mimics, Organ-Risk Assessment
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis built from a compatible clinical-radiologic pattern, exclusion of important mimics and tissue confirmation when necessary. The NP priority is identifying organ-threatening disease—especially cardiac, neurologic, ocular or severe pulmonary involvement—rather than treating every radiographic abnormality with corticosteroids.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, cough/dyspnea, erythema nodosum, uveitis, hypercalcemia and constitutional symptoms can occur.
Sarcoidosis may involve eyes, heart, nervous system, skin, liver and other organs, so a lung-only assessment can miss high-risk disease.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, occupational/environmental granulomatous disease and other inflammatory disorders can mimic sarcoidosis.
Asymptomatic/stable pulmonary findings may be observed; organ-threatening or progressive disease changes the treatment threshold.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms/function plus palpitations, syncope, neurologic symptoms, visual symptoms, skin findings, calcium-related symptoms and occupational/travel/infectious exposures.
Review medications and comorbidities that influence corticosteroid/immunosuppressive risk.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary function to define pulmonary involvement; obtain ECG and organ-specific testing when symptoms/risk suggest extrapulmonary disease.
Tissue biopsy is used when diagnostic certainty is needed and a safe accessible site exists; microbiologic/malignancy evaluation must reflect the differential.
Avoid using serum ACE alone to diagnose or exclude sarcoidosis.
management: Observe selected stable/asymptomatic disease with structured follow-up.
Use specialist-guided corticosteroid or steroid-sparing therapy for progressive, symptomatic or organ-threatening disease.
Urgently refer suspected cardiac sarcoidosis, neurosarcoidosis, sight-threatening ocular disease or rapidly progressive respiratory impairment.
medicationSafety: Before significant immunosuppression, screen for latent/active infections according to current CTS ILD/immunosuppression guidance and drug-specific standards.
Long-term corticosteroid therapy requires glucose, BP, bone, infection and other toxicity prevention/monitoring.
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can improve spontaneously and that treatment is based on symptoms, progression and organ risk—not the x-ray alone.
Review vitamin D/calcium supplements before routine use when hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria is a concern.
followUp: Trend symptoms, pulmonary function and imaging as appropriate, and maintain organ-specific surveillance based on the disease pattern.
Reassess diagnosis if the course becomes atypical or fails to respond as expected.
examTrap: Diagnosing sarcoidosis from hilar adenopathy plus a high ACE level without excluding infection/malignancy—or treating an asymptomatic stable patient solely because imaging is abnormal.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis treatment follows organ risk and progression, not radiographic stage alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Interstitial Lung Disease guidance/current ILD standards

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Preserve Function Through Specialized Multidisciplinary Care
bottomLine: Adults with cystic fibrosis need longitudinal specialty-centre care that integrates airway clearance, infection surveillance, nutrition, CFTR-modulator eligibility, diabetes/liver/bone complications and transition planning. The NP should recognize pulmonary exacerbation and drug-interaction/toxicity problems early, but complex CF antimicrobial and modulator decisions remain coordinated with the CF team.
recognize: Increasing cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, appetite/weight loss or lung-function decline can signal pulmonary exacerbation even without dramatic fever.
CF is multisystem: pancreatic insufficiency, CF-related diabetes, liver disease, infertility/reproductive issues, sinus disease and low bone density are common management domains.
differentiate: A CF pulmonary exacerbation may reflect infection but treatment is guided by prior airway microbiology and the patient's longitudinal pattern.
New hemoptysis, pneumothorax, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial disease requires a different specialty pathway than routine exacerbation.
assessment: Assess change from baseline symptoms, sputum, hemoptysis, weight/nutrition, airway-clearance adherence, CFTR modulator use/adherence, prior organisms/resistance, diabetes symptoms and access to CF-centre care.
Review pregnancy planning and major drug interactions because modulator/antimicrobial decisions may need specialist adjustment.
workup: Use sputum/airway microbiology and spirometry/lung-function trend through the CF care pathway.
Monitor nutrition, glucose/CF-related diabetes, liver health, fat-soluble vitamins and bone health according to current CF standards and individual risk.
management: Maintain individualized airway clearance, exercise/nutrition support, pancreatic enzyme/vitamin therapy where indicated and CFTR-modulator therapy for eligible patients through the CF program.
Pulmonary exacerbations require prompt CF-team contact and organism/history-informed antimicrobial planning; severe decline, hypoxemia or major complications require hospital-level care.
Coordinate adolescent-to-adult transition and reproductive planning proactively.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators and many antimicrobials have important interaction and organ-monitoring requirements; use current Canadian product/specialty guidance.
Do not prescribe prolonged broad-spectrum therapy without checking the patient's microbiology, resistance history and CF-centre plan.
counselling: Reinforce infection-prevention practices and the importance of CF-centre follow-up even when symptoms are stable.
Use shared decision-making about treatment burden, fertility/pregnancy and advanced-care planning as disease severity changes.
followUp: Ensure CF-centre review after exacerbations and close the loop on cultures, lung-function changes and complication screening.
Track treatment burden/adherence without framing missed complex regimens as simple noncompliance.
examTrap: Treating an adult with CF as routine COPD/bronchiectasis and choosing antibiotics without prior CF microbiology or specialty coordination.
oneLinePearl: Adult CF is specialized longitudinal multisystem care, not just chronic lung infection.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada Canadian Guidelines for CF Care and Standards of Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada 2024 CFTR Modulator Clinical Consensus Guideline

title: Mechanical Ventilation Basics for the NP: Oxygenation, Ventilation, Pressure, and the Patient
bottomLine: A ventilator setting is not a diagnosis. The NP must connect oxygenation, ventilation, airway pressures, synchrony and hemodynamics to the patient's disease, immediately recognize dangerous deterioration, and work within the critical-care team rather than making isolated setting changes without reassessment.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP primarily influence oxygenation, while minute ventilation influences CO2 clearance; tidal volume, respiratory rate and patient effort determine the actual physiology.
Sudden high-pressure alarms can signal secretions, biting, bronchospasm, tube kinking or reduced compliance; sudden low-pressure/low-volume alarms can signal disconnection or leak.
differentiate: Peak pressure rises with airway resistance or compliance problems, whereas plateau pressure better reflects alveolar/static pressure when measured correctly.
Hypoxemia despite high support should trigger a cause search—tube displacement, pneumothorax, atelectasis, edema, mucus plugging or disease progression—not reflex FiO2 escalation alone.
assessment: Assess the patient first: airway/tube position, chest rise, breath sounds, oxygen saturation, hemodynamics, mental status/sedation, secretions and ventilator synchrony.
Review ABG/VBG when indicated, current settings, exhaled tidal volume, airway pressures and recent changes.
workup: Use blood gas, chest imaging, bedside ultrasound and other testing according to the deterioration pattern.
When lung-protective ventilation is indicated, use predicted/ideal-body-weight-based tidal-volume principles and monitor pressures rather than actual body weight alone.
management: For sudden instability, disconnecting from assumptions is more important than changing a number: call for critical-care/RT support, ensure oxygenation/ventilation, hand-ventilate when appropriate, and rapidly evaluate tube/circuit/pneumothorax/secretions.
Use disease-specific lung-protective, obstructive-lung or weaning strategies under the ICU protocol/team.
Daily readiness for sedation reduction, spontaneous-breathing assessment and liberation should be addressed when clinically appropriate.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, opioids and neuromuscular blockers can obscure neurologic/respiratory assessment and require explicit indication and monitoring.
Aggressive PEEP or positive-pressure changes can worsen hypotension/right-heart compromise; reassess hemodynamics after meaningful changes.
redFlags: Absent unilateral breath sounds/tension pneumothorax concern
Unable to ventilate or rapidly rising CO2/acidemia
counselling: For patients/families, explain the goal of mechanical ventilation as temporary physiologic support when appropriate, and communicate liberation/prognosis decisions through the critical-care team.
followUp: Trend gas exchange, pressures, synchrony, sedation, hemodynamics and readiness for liberation rather than judging success from oxygen saturation alone.
Document the cause and response to acute ventilator deterioration in closed-loop handoff.
examTrap: Responding to sudden ventilator desaturation by increasing FiO2 and walking away without checking the patient, tube, circuit and pneumothorax/secretions.
oneLinePearl: When the ventilated patient crashes, assess the patient and airway before the screen.
sourceBasis: Canadian Critical Care Society mechanical ventilation education/guideline resources
Canadian Thoracic Society home/non-invasive ventilation guidance where applicable

title: Asthma-COPD Overlap: Preserve Asthma Safety While Treating Fixed Airflow Disease
bottomLine: When a patient has persistent airflow obstruction plus convincing asthma features, do not treat them like COPD alone. Confirm spirometric obstruction, clarify asthma history/eosinophilic features/exacerbations, preserve inhaled-corticosteroid-containing therapy when asthma is present, and add long-acting bronchodilator treatment according to symptoms and exacerbation risk.
recognize: Features supporting asthma include variable symptoms, earlier-onset disease, atopy, marked variability/reversibility and prior asthma diagnosis; COPD features include persistent obstruction, smoking/biomass exposure and progressive exertional symptoms.
The overlap label is less important than identifying the asthma component because LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma.
differentiate: Asthma with persistent obstruction is not automatically COPD, and COPD with eosinophilia is not automatically asthma.
Dyspnea from heart failure, bronchiectasis, obesity/deconditioning, ILD or pulmonary vascular disease can coexist and should not be forced into an overlap label.
assessment: Review symptom variability, childhood/adult asthma history, atopy, smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, exacerbations/hospitalizations, eosinophil history, inhaler use/technique and pneumonia risk.
Assess whether the patient is actually taking an inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimen when asthma features are convincing.
workup: Perform quality spirometry with bronchodilator testing and use prior lung-function variability when available.
Use eosinophils/allergy testing selectively to support phenotype/therapy questions; obtain imaging or other testing when another diagnosis is plausible.
management: If asthma is present, maintain an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing regimen and do not use LABA alone.
Add LABA/LAMA and optimize COPD-style bronchodilation according to symptoms/exacerbations while continuing asthma-safe anti-inflammatory therapy.
Treat smoking/vaping exposure, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/exercise and comorbid rhinitis/GERD/OSA where relevant; refer severe or diagnostically uncertain disease to respirology.
medicationSafety: Avoid LABA monotherapy when asthma is part of the phenotype.
Balance inhaled-corticosteroid benefit against pneumonia/thrush/other risks, but do not withdraw asthma-protective anti-inflammatory therapy solely because the patient also meets COPD criteria.
redFlags: Severe exacerbation with inability to speak or impending respiratory failure
Uncertain diagnosis with atypical imaging/systemic features
counselling: Teach device technique and adherence using the exact prescribed inhalers; confirm the patient understands which controller is daily and which reliever strategy applies.
Provide an individualized action plan for worsening symptoms.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, exacerbations, inhaler technique, adherence and spirometry/functional status after treatment changes.
If the asthma/COPD classification remains uncertain or control is poor, obtain specialist review rather than escalating inhalers indefinitely.
examTrap: Using LABA monotherapy in a patient with convincing asthma plus fixed obstruction because the spirometry also meets COPD criteria.
oneLinePearl: Overlap changes bronchodilation, but the asthma component keeps inhaled corticosteroid safety rules in force.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current Asthma guideline
Canadian Thoracic Society current COPD guidance and care tools
